problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis $B$ of $\text{span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}.$

activity_context.topic_title: Finding a Basis of a Span

examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors by Identifying Pivot Columns

examples.worked_solution:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 15 \\ 2 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $3$rd columns are pivot columns, while the $2$nd column is a non-pivot column.

Remember that we need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ that is to say,

feedback.problem: Consider the vectors ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}],$ and ${a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ Find a basis of $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$  by inspection.
feedback.worked_solution:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that ${a}_{2}$ is a linear combination of vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{a}_{2}=2\cdot {a}_{1}+0\cdot {a}_{3}
$$

Consequently, the vector ${a}_{2}$ can be removed from $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ without changing the span. So $S=\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is spanned by just ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}.$ 

Lastly, note that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is ${{a}_{1},{a}_{3}},$ that is to say,

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}},{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}}.
$$
